revision.text: Meiji Jingu, located in [[Tokyo]],[[Japan]] is the [[Shinto]] shrine dedicated to the souls of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Emperess Shoken]]. Emperor Meiji passed away in 1912 and Empress Shoken in 1914. After the demise of the Emperor and Empress, this shrine was constructed to venerate them. Their souls were enshrined on November 1, 1920. The shrine grounds consists of three areas: Naien, or the inner precinct, centered on the shrine buildings; Gaien, or the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery and sports facilities; and the Meiji Memorial Hall. These areas are covered by an evergreen forest of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. This 700,000 square-meter forest is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area centre of Tokyo.

[[Image:MeijiShrine1202.jpg|thumb|300px|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined.]] '''Meiji Jingu''' (明治神宮), located in [[Tokyo]], [[Japan]] near [[Harajuku Station]] is the [[Jinja (shrine)|Shinto shrine]] dedicated to the souls of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Emperor Meiji|Empress Shoken]]. Emperor Meiji passed away in [[1912]] and Empress Shoken in 1914. After the demise of the Emperor and Empress, this shrine was constructed to venerate them. Their souls were enshrined on November 1, [[1920]].
The shrine grounds consists of three areas: Naien, or the inner precinct, centered on the shrine buildings; Gaien, or the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery and sports facilities; and the Meiji Memorial Hall. These areas are covered by an evergreen forest of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. This 700,000 square-meter forest is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo.

revision.text:
[[Image:MeijiShrine1202.jpg|thumb|300px|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined.]] '''Meiji Jingu''' (明治神宮), located in [[Tokyo]], [[Japan]] near [[Harajuku Station]] is the [[Jinja (shrine)|Shinto shrine]] dedicated to the souls of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Emperor Meiji|Empress Shoken]]. Emperor Meiji passed away in [[1912]] and Empress Shoken in 1914. After the demise of the Emperor and Empress, this shrine was constructed to venerate them. Their souls were enshrined on November 1, [[1920]]. The original building was destroyed during [[World War II]]. The present shrine was completed in October, 1958.
The shrine grounds consist of two areas: *Naien, or the inner precinct/garden, centered on the shrine buildings, which include a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress enshrined here. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. *Gaien, or the outer precinct/garden, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings.
These areas are covered by an evergreen forest of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. This 700,000 square-meter forest (about 175 acres) is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo.
The shrine was built in a garden area where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken sometimes visited. The shrine was built in the [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress from [[Kiso]], which is considered the best lumber produced in Japan.

[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{cite web |url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}} When Emperor Meiji died in 1912 and Empress Shōken in 1914, the [[Japanese people]] wished to pay their respects to the two influential Japanese figures. It was for this reason that Meiji Shrine was constructed and their souls enshrined on [[November 1]], [[1920]].{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == History == After the emperor's death in 1692, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1770, completed in 1771, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{cite web |url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]}} The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == Shrine complex == Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. This 700,000 square-meter forest (about 175 acres) is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is comprised of two major areas: === Naien === The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. === Gaien === The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Image gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined. [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{cite web |url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}} When Emperor Meiji died in 1912 and Empress Shōken in 1914, the [[Japanese people]] wished to pay their respects to the two influential Japanese figures. It was for this reason that Meiji Shrine was constructed and their souls enshrined on [[November 1]], [[1920]].{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == History == After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{cite web |url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]}} The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == Shrine complex == Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is comprised of two major areas: === Naien === The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. === Gaien === The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Image gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined. [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{cite web |url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}} When Emperor Meiji died in 1912 and Empress Shōken in 1914, the [[Japanese people]] wished to pay their respects to the two influential Japanese figures. It was for this reason that Meiji Shrine was constructed and their souls enshrined on [[November 1]], [[1920]].{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == History == After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{cite web |url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]}} The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan." [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{cite web |url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}} When Emperor Meiji died in 1912 and Empress Shōken in 1914, the [[Japanese people]] wished to pay their respects to the two influential Japanese figures. It was for this reason that Meiji Shrine was constructed and their souls enshrined on [[November 1]], [[1920]].{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == History == After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{cite web |url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan." [http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. == Shrine complex == Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is comprised of two major areas: === Naien === The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. === Gaien === The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Image gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined. It was for this reason that Meiji Shrine was constructed and their souls enshrined on [[November 1]], [[1920]].{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == History == After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{cite web |url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan." [http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. == Shrine complex == Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: === Naien === The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. === Gaien === The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Image gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined. [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{cite web |url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}} When Emperor Meiji died in 1912 and Empress Shōken in 1914, the [[Japanese people]] wished to pay their respects to the two influential Japanese figures. It was for this reason that Meiji Shrine was constructed and their souls enshrined on November 1, 1920.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == History == After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{cite web |url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan." [http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. In January 2010, [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]] demonstrated the same respect when he concluded his visit to Japan with a visit of the shrine.http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html == Shrine complex == Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: === Naien === The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. === Gaien === The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Image gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined. Image:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine. Image:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu. {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Meiji Shrine
明治神宮 | image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg | width = | caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex | type = Imperial Shrine | dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] | founded = November 1, 1920 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Harajuku]],Tokyo, is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{cite web |url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}} When Emperor Meiji died in 1912 and Empress Shōken in 1914, the [[Japanese people]] wished to pay their respects to the two influential Japanese figures. It was for this reason that Meiji Shrine was constructed and their souls enshrined on November 1, 1920.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == History == After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{cite web |url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan." [http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. In January 2010, [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]] demonstrated the same respect when he concluded his visit to Japan with a visit of the shrine.http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html == Shrine complex == Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: === Naien === The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. === Gaien === The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Image gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined. Image:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine. Image:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu. {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Meiji Shrine
明治神宮 | image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg | width = | caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex | type = Imperial Shrine | dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] | founded = November 1, 1920 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{cite web |url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}} When Emperor Meiji died in 1912 and Empress Shōken in 1914, the [[Japanese people]] wished to pay their respects to the two influential Japanese figures. It was for this reason that Meiji Shrine was constructed and their souls enshrined on November 1, 1920.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == History == After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{cite web |url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan." [http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. In January 2010, [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]] demonstrated the same respect when he concluded his visit to Japan with a visit of the shrine.http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html == Shrine complex == Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: === Naien === The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. === Gaien === The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Meiji Shrine
明治神宮 | image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg | width = | caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex | type = Imperial Shrine | dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] | founded = November 1, 1920 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{cite web |url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}} When Emperor Meiji died in 1912 and Empress Shōken in 1914, the Japanese people wished to pay their respects to the two influential figures. It was for this reason that Meiji Shrine was constructed and their souls enshrined on November 1, 1920.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22}} == History == After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{cite web |url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{cite web |url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan."[http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. In January 2010, [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]] demonstrated the same respect when he concluded his visit to Japan with a visit of the shrine.http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html == Shrine complex == Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many people both as a spiritual home of the people and as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: === Naien === The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. === Gaien === The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Image gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined Image:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine Image:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu Image:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine Image:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself Image:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors Image:CIMG4989.JPG | Women signing prayers in main yard Image:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} * [[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] * [[List of Shinto shrines]] * [[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [http://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{Commons category|Meiji Shrine}} * [http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ Official English site] Requires Flash. * [http://gmap.jp/shop-7467.html Meiji Shrine English map] * [http://www.haejunghofman.com/2009/02/meiji-jingu/ Meiji Shrine Panorama] {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title}} {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:1920 establishments]] [[Category:1958 architecture]] [[Category:Shibuya, Tokyo]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]] [[ar:ميجي جينغو]] [[de:Meiji-Schrein]] [[fr:Meiji-jingū]] [[ko:메이지 신궁]] [[it:Santuario Meiji]] [[hu:Meidzsi-szentély]] [[ja:明治神宮]] [[no:Meiji-helligdommen]] [[ru:Храм Мэйдзи]] [[sr:Храм Меиђи]] [[sv:Meiji-templet]] [[uk:Святилище Мейдзі]] [[zh:明治神宫]]

{{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Meiji Shrine
明治神宮 | image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg | width = | caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex | type = Imperial Shrine | dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] | founded = November 1, 1920 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} ==History== After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan."[http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. In January 2010, [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]] demonstrated the same respect when he concluded his visit to Japan with a visit of the shrine.http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}}. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Image gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined Image:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine Image:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu Image:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine Image:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself Image:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors Image:CIMG4989.JPG | Women signing prayers in main yard Image:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} * [[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] * [[List of Shinto shrines]] * [[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [http://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{Commons category|Meiji Shrine}} * [http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ Official English site] Requires Flash. * [http://gmap.jp/shop-7467.html Meiji Shrine English map] * [http://www.haejunghofman.com/2009/02/meiji-jingu/ Meiji Shrine Panorama] {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title}} {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:1920 establishments]] [[Category:1958 architecture]] [[Category:Shibuya, Tokyo]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]] [[ar:ميجي جينغو]] [[de:Meiji-Schrein]] [[fa:معبد میجی]] [[fr:Meiji-jingū]] [[ko:메이지 신궁]] [[it:Santuario Meiji]] [[hu:Meidzsi-szentély]] [[ja:明治神宮]] [[no:Meiji-helligdommen]] [[ru:Храм Мэйдзи]] [[sr:Храм Меиђи]] [[sv:Meiji-templet]] [[uk:Святилище Мейдзі]] [[zh:明治神宫]]

An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915, and the shrine was built in the traditional [[Nagarezukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan."[http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. In January 2010, [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]] demonstrated the same respect when he concluded his visit to Japan with a visit of the shrine.http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}}. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. 明治神宮 | image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg | width = | caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex | type = Imperial Shrine | dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] | founded = November 1, 1920 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} ==History== After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan."[http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. In January 2010, [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]] demonstrated the same respect when he concluded his visit to Japan with a visit of the shrine.http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium, and is seen as the center of Japanese sports{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}}. It also includes the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Image gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined Image:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine Image:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu Image:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine Image:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself Image:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg| Women signing prayers in main yard Image:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama Image:Hitlerjugend visit to Meiji Shrine purification queue 1938.jpg|A delegation of the [[Hitlerjugend]] visits the Meji shrine in 1938 Image:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi park]] ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} * [[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] * [[List of Shinto shrines]] * [[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Meiji Shrine
明治神宮 | image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg | width = | caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex | type = Imperial Shrine | dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] | founded = November 1, 1920 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} ==History== After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan."[http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. In January 2010, [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]] demonstrated the same respect when he concluded his visit to Japan with a visit of the shrine.http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined Image:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine Image:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu Image:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine Image:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself Image:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg| Women signing prayers in main yard Image:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama Image:Hitlerjugend visit to Meiji Shrine purification queue 1938.jpg|A delegation of the [[Hitler Youth|Hitlerjugend]] visits the Meiji shrine in 1938 Image:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi park]] ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} * [[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] * [[List of Shinto shrines]] * [[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Meiji Shrine
明治神宮 | image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg | width = | caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex | type = Imperial Shrine | dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] | founded = November 1, 1920 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} ==History== [[File:Yabusame 05.jpg|thumb|In November 2001, [[Yabusame]] demonstrated for the president [[George W. Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style and is made up primarily of Japanese cypress and copper. It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine was brought into the flow of current events with the 2009 visit of [[United States Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]]. After arriving in Tokyo on her first foreign trip representing the newly elected [[United States President|President]] [[Barack Obama]], she made her way to this shrine in advance of meetings with Japan's leaders to show her "respect toward history and the culture of Japan."[http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?sectionName=WorldSectionPage&id=c2fab7b6-7956-400c-92a1-a7738ba4235f&MatchID1=4924&TeamID1=4&TeamID2=2&MatchType1=1&SeriesID1=1244&PrimaryID=4924&Headline=Clinton+visits+Tokyo+shrine "Clinton visits Tokyo shrine,"] ''Hindustani Times.'' February 17, 2009. In January 2010, [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]] demonstrated the same respect when he concluded his visit to Japan with a visit of the shrine.{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century. Today it is used for Shinto weddings. ==Gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined Image:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine Image:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu Image:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine Image:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself Image:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg| Women signing prayers in main yard Image:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama Image:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi park]] ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} * [[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] * [[List of Shinto shrines]] * [[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [http://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{Commons category|Meiji Shrine}} * [http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ Official English site] Requires Flash. * [http://gmap.jp/shop-7467.html Meiji Shrine English map] * [http://www.haejunghofman.com/2009/02/meiji-jingu/ Meiji Shrine Panorama] {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title}} {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:1920 establishments in Japan]] [[Category:Religious buildings completed in 1958]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Shibuya]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]]

[[Empress Shoken]] | founded = November 1, 1920 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} ==History== [[File:Yabusame 05.jpg|thumb|In November 2001, [[Yabusame]] demonstrated for the president [[George W. Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October, 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign leaders, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]], {{cite news |url=http://m.hindustantimes.com/world-news/clinton-visits-tokyo-shrine/article1-379967.aspx |title=Clinton visits Tokyo shrine |work=Hindustan Times |date= 17 February 2009}} and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of 700,000 square-meters (about 175 acres). This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall, which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the Meiji Constitution in the late 19th century.
