{{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Meiji Shrine
明治神宮 | image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg | width = | caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex | type = Imperial Shrine | dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] | founded = November 1, 1920 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at Fushimi-momoyama south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Yabusame 05.jpg|thumb|In November 2001, [[Yabusame]] demonstrated for the president [[George W. Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = http://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign leaders, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]],{{cite news |url=http://m.hindustantimes.com/world-news/clinton-visits-tokyo-shrine/article1-379967.aspx |title=Clinton visits Tokyo shrine |work=Hindustan Times |date= 17 February 2009}} and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. ==Gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor is enshrined Image:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine Image:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu Image:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine Image:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself Image:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg| Women signing prayers in main yard Image:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama Image:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi park]] ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} * [[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] * [[List of Shinto shrines]] * [[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [http://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{Commons category|Meiji Shrine}} * [http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ Official English site] Requires Flash. * [http://gmap.jp/shop-7467.html Meiji Shrine English map] * [http://www.haejunghofman.com/2009/02/meiji-jingu/ Meiji Shrine Panorama] {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title}} {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:1920 establishments in Japan]] [[Category:Religious buildings completed in 1958]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Shibuya]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]]

{{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Meiji Shrine
明治神宮 | image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg | width = | caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex | type = Imperial Shrine | dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] | founded = November 1, 1920 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 | website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at Fushimi-momoyama south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Yabusame 05.jpg|thumb|In November 2001, [[Yabusame]] demonstrated for the president [[George W. Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]],{{cite news |url=http://m.hindustantimes.com/world-news/clinton-visits-tokyo-shrine/article1-379967.aspx |title=Clinton visits Tokyo shrine |work=Hindustan Times |date= 17 February 2009}} and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. ==Gallery== Image:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor eats food Image:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine Image:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu Image:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine Image:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself Image:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg| Women signing prayers in main yard Image:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama Image:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi park]] ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} * [[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] * [[List of Shinto shrines]] * [[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{Commons category|Meiji Shrine}} * [http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ Official English site] Requires Flash. * [http://gmap.jp/shop-7467.html Meiji Shrine English map] * [http://www.haejunghofman.com/2009/02/meiji-jingu/ Meiji Shrine Panorama] {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title}} {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:1920 establishments in Japan]] [[Category:Religious buildings completed in 1958]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Shibuya]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]]

Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. {{Infobox Shinto shrine |name = Tōdai-hi
明治神宮 |image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg |width = |caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex |type = Imperial Shrine |dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] |founded = November 1, 1920 |closed = |founder = |priest = |address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō
[[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya, Tokyo|Shibuya-ku]]
[[Tokyo]] 151-0053 |phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 |website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya, Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto]] [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at Fushimi-momoyama, south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Yabusame 05.jpg|thumb|In November 2001, [[Yabusame]] demonstrated for the president [[George W. Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]],{{cite news |url=http://m.hindustantimes.com/world-news/clinton-visits-tokyo-shrine/article1-379967.aspx |title=Clinton visits Tokyo shrine |work=Hindustan Times |date= 17 February 2009}} and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. ==Gallery== File:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor eats food File:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine File:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu File:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine File:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself File:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg| Women signing prayers in main yard File:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama File:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi park]] File:Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine.jpg|thumb|Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} *[[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== *[[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]]|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV|archivedate=2009-11-01|deadurl=yes}} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]],{{cite news |url=http://m.hindustantimes.com/world-news/clinton-visits-tokyo-shrine/article1-379967.aspx |title=Clinton visits Tokyo shrine |work=Hindustan Times |date= 17 February 2009}} and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. ==Gallery== File:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor eats food File:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine File:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu File:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine File:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself File:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg| Women signing prayers in main yard File:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama File:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi park]] File:Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine.jpg|thumb|Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} *[[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== *[[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. {{Infobox Shinto shrine |name = Meiji Shrine
明治神宮 |image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg |width = |caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex |type = Imperial Shrine |dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] |founded = November 1, 1920 |closed = |founder = |priest = |address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 |phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 |website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at Fushimi-momoyama, south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Yabusame 05.jpg|thumb|In November 2001, [[Yabusame]] demonstrated for the president [[George W. Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archiveurl=https://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV?url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archivedate=2009-11-01 |deadurl=yes |df= }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]],{{cite news |url=http://m.hindustantimes.com/world-news/clinton-visits-tokyo-shrine/article1-379967.aspx |title=Clinton visits Tokyo shrine |work=Hindustan Times |date= 17 February 2009}} and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. [[Empress Shoken]] |founded = November 1, 1920 |closed = |founder = |priest = |address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 |phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 |website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at Fushimi-momoyama, south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Yabusame 05.jpg|thumb|In November 2001, [[Yabusame]] demonstrated for the president [[George W. Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archiveurl=https://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV?url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archivedate=2009-11-01 |deadurl=yes |df= }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]],{{cite news |url=http://m.hindustantimes.com/world-news/clinton-visits-tokyo-shrine/article1-379967.aspx |title=Clinton visits Tokyo shrine |work=Hindustan Times |date= 17 February 2009}} and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. ==Gallery== File:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor eats food File:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine File:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu File:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine File:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself File:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg|Women signing prayers in main yard File:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama File:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi park]] File:Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine.jpg|Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} *[[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== *[[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. {{Infobox Shinto shrine |name = Meiji Shrine
明治神宮 |image = MeijiShrineTorii1167.jpg |width = |caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex |type = Imperial Shrine |dedication = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] |founded = November 1, 1920 |closed = |founder = |priest = | location_map = Japan | coordinates ={{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} |address = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 |phone = +81 (03) 3379-5511 |website = http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at Fushimi-momoyama, south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Yabusame 05.jpg|thumb|In November 2001, [[Yabusame]] demonstrated for the president [[George W. Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archiveurl=https://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV?url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archivedate=2009-11-01 |deadurl=yes |df= }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]], and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} On the eve of new year, Japanese usually visit a shinto shrine to prepare for the worship - [[Hatsumōde]] (初詣) of the new year. Meiji Shrine is the most popular location in Tokyo by Hatsumōde. ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. ==Gallery== File:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor eats food File:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine File:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu File:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine File:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself File:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg|Women signing prayers in main yard File:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama File:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi park]] File:Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine.jpg|Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} *[[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== *[[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{Commons category|Meiji Shrine}} *[http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ Official English site] Requires Flash. *[http://gmap.jp/shop-7467.html Meiji Shrine English map] *[http://www.annees-de-pelerinage.com/meiji-shrine-tokyo/ Meiji Shrine Pictures & Travel Guide] *[https://www.yokosojapan.net/article.php/20180201meijishrine_editor_en]　Practical　guide　for travelers {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:1920 establishments in Japan]] [[Category:Religious buildings completed in 1958]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Shibuya]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Japan destroyed during World War II]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]]

[[Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at Fushimi-momoyama, south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Yabusame 05.jpg|thumb|In November 2001, [[Yabusame]] demonstrated for the president [[George W. Bush]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editorlink1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archiveurl=https://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV?url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archivedate=2009-11-01 |deadurl=yes |df= }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]], and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} On the eve of new year, Japanese usually visit a shinto shrine to prepare for the worship - [[Hatsumōde]] (初詣) of the new year. Meiji Shrine is the most popular location in Tokyo by Hatsumōde. ==Shrine complex== Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. ==Gallery== File:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary where the Meiji emperor eats food File:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine File:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|Another view of the [[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu File:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine File:MeijiShrine1.jpg|The shrine itself File:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg|Women signing prayers in main yard File:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama File:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi Park]] File:Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine.jpg|Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} *[[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== *[[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{Commons category|Meiji Shrine}} *[http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ Official English site] Requires Flash. *[http://gmap.jp/shop-7467.html Meiji Shrine English map] *[http://www.annees-de-pelerinage.com/meiji-shrine-tokyo/ Meiji Shrine Pictures & Travel Guide] *[https://www.yokosojapan.net/article.php/20180201meijishrine_editor_en]　Practical　guide　for travelers {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:1920 establishments in Japan]] [[Category:Religious buildings completed in 1958]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Shibuya]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Japan destroyed during World War II]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]]

An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editorlink1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archiveurl=https://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV?url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archivedate=2009-11-01 |deadurl=yes |df= }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]], and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} On the eve of new year, Japanese usually visit a Shinto shrine to prepare for the worship - [[Hatsumōde]] (初詣) of the new year. Meiji Shrine is the most popular location in Japan for hatsumōde. ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of [[Tokyo]]. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. ==Gallery== File:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary File:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine File:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|[[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu File:Courtyard_of_Meiji_Shrine2.jpg|Torii at hte courtyard of Meiji-jingu File:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine File:MeijiShrine1.jpg|In front of Meiji shrine File:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg|Women signing prayers in main courtyard File:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama File:Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine.jpg|Barrels of [[Burgundy]] from France was donated to the Meiji-shrine File:明治神宮ー武道.JPG|Ancient Martial Arts Dedication at the Festival of Autumn (November 2, 2012) File:明治神宮ー火縄銃.JPG|Ancient Martial Arrangement Firework Gun dedication at the Festival of Autumn (November 2, 2012) File:明治神宮ー流鏑馬.JPG|Demon Flower Vacation at the Festival of Autumn (November 2, 2012) File:Meiji-Shrine-Innergarden-02.jpg|Meiji Shrine Gyoen (inner garden) File:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi Park]] ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} *[[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== *[[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{Commons category|Meiji Shrine}} *[http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ Official English site] Requires Flash. *[http://gmap.jp/shop-7467.html Meiji Shrine English map] *[http://www.annees-de-pelerinage.com/meiji-shrine-tokyo/ Meiji Shrine Pictures & Travel Guide] *[https://www.yokosojapan.net/article.php/20180201meijishrine_editor_en]　Practical　guide　for travelers {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:1920 establishments in Japan]] [[Category:Religious buildings completed in 1958]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Shibuya]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Japan destroyed during World War II]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]]

[[Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at Fushimi-momoyama, south of [[Kyoto]]. s location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editorlink1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archiveurl=https://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV?url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archivedate=2009-11-01 |deadurl=yes |df= }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]], and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} On the eve of new year, Japanese usually visit a Shinto shrine to prepare for the worship - [[Hatsumōde]] (初詣) of the new year. Meiji Shrine is the most popular location in Japan for hatsumōde. ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of [[Tokyo]]. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. ==Gallery== File:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary File:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine File:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|[[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu File:Courtyard_of_Meiji_Shrine2.jpg|Torii at the courtyard of Meiji-jingu File:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine File:MeijiShrine1.jpg|In front of Meiji shrine File:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg|Women signing prayers in main courtyard File:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama File:Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine.jpg|Barrels of [[Burgundy]] from France was donated to the Meiji-shrine File:明治神宮ー武道.JPG|Ancient Martial Arts Dedication at the Festival of Autumn (November 2, 2012) File:明治神宮ー火縄銃.JPG|Ancient Martial Arrangement Firework Gun dedication at the Festival of Autumn (November 2, 2012) File:明治神宮ー流鏑馬.JPG|Demon Flower Vacation at the Festival of Autumn (November 2, 2012) File:Meiji-Shrine-Innergarden-02.jpg|Meiji Shrine Gyoen (inner garden) File:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi Park]] ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} *[[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== *[[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{Commons category|Meiji Shrine}} *[http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ Official English site] Requires Flash. *[http://gmap.jp/shop-7467.html Meiji Shrine English map] *[http://www.annees-de-pelerinage.com/meiji-shrine-tokyo/ Meiji Shrine Pictures & Travel Guide] *[https://www.yokosojapan.net/article.php/20180201meijishrine_editor_en]　Practical　guide　for travelers {{Shinto shrine}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:1920 establishments in Japan]] [[Category:Religious buildings completed in 1958]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Shibuya]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Japan destroyed during World War II]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]]

{{Infobox religious building | name = Meiji Shrine | native_name =明治神宮 | image = Meiji-Torii-2018.jpg | caption = ''[[Torii]]'' leading to the Meiji Shrine complex | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Imperial Shrine | deity = [[Emperor Meiji]]
[[Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''', located in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], is the [[Shinto shrine]] that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at Fushimi-momoyama, south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Yabusame 05.jpg|thumb|In November 2001, [[Yabusame]] demonstrated for former president [[George W. Bush]] and prime minister [[Junichiro Koizumi]] at Meiji Jingu shrine.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editorlink1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151&lpg=PA151#v=onepage&f=false|accessdate=29 March 2015}} It was formally dedicated in 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926.{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |accessdate=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archiveurl=https://www.webcitation.org/5kx7DD0qV?url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archivedate=2009-11-01 |deadurl=yes |df= }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |accessdate=2008-03-22 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archivedate = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]], and [[German Foreign Minister]] [[Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archivedate=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} On the eve of new year, Japanese usually visit a Shinto shrine to prepare for the worship - [[Hatsumōde]] (初詣) of the new year. Meiji Shrine is the most popular location in Japan for hatsumōde. ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of [[Tokyo]]. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the National Stadium ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]] and later, since 1956, on the same site, [[Olympic Stadium (Tokyo)|Tokyo Olympic Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. ==Gallery== File:MeijiShrine2.jpg|The central sanctuary File:MeijiShrineSakeBarrels1227.jpg|Barrels of [[sake]] (''nihonshu'') donated to the Meiji Shrine File:Meiji-jingu_torii.JPG|[[torii]] at the entrance to Meiji-jingu File:Courtyard_of_Meiji_Shrine2.jpg|Torii at the courtyard of Meiji-jingu File:MeijiShrinePriestsMaidens1187.jpg|Priests and maidens wear traditional dress in preparation for a wedding at the Meiji Shrine File:MeijiShrine1.jpg|In front of Meiji shrine File:MeijiShrine3.jpg|Prayers left by visitors File:Meiji Shrine Tokyo, Japan.jpg|Women signing prayers in main courtyard File:Meiji shrine.jpg|Meiji Shrine main yard panorama File:Meiji Shrine Barrels of wine.jpg|Barrels of [[Burgundy]] from France was donated to the Meiji-shrine File:明治神宮ー武道.JPG|Ancient Martial Arts Dedication at the Festival of Autumn (November 2, 2012) File:明治神宮ー火縄銃.JPG|Ancient Martial Arrangement Firework Gun dedication at the Festival of Autumn (November 2, 2012) File:明治神宮ー流鏑馬.JPG|Demon Flower Vacation at the Festival of Autumn (November 2, 2012) File:Meiji-Shrine-Innergarden-02.jpg|Meiji Shrine Gyoen (inner garden) File:Yoyogi_Park_from_Hyatt.jpg|Meiji Shrine with [[Yoyogi Park]] ==See also== {{Portal|Tokyo}} *[[Meiji Jingu Stadium]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of Jingū]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|2}} ==References== *[[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&dq=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan&client=firefox-a&pgis=1 ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{Commons category|Meiji Shrine}} *[http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/ Official English site] Requires Flash. *[http://gmap.jp/shop-7467.html Meiji Shrine English map] *[http://www.annees-de-pelerinage.com/meiji-shrine-tokyo/ Meiji Shrine Pictures & Travel Guide] *[https://www.yokosojapan.net/article.php/20180201meijishrine_editor_en]　Practical　guide　for travelers {{Shinto shrine}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:1920 establishments in Japan]] [[Category:Religious buildings and structures completed in 1958]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Shibuya]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Japan destroyed during World War II]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]]
