{{short description|Shinto shrine in Tokyo, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Meiji Shrine | native_name = 明治神宮 | image = Meiji_Jingu_2023-3.jpg | caption = Meiji Jingu Shrine Main Hall in 2023 | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Imperial Shrine | deity = [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]
[[:en:Empress Shoken|Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''' is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[:en:Empress Shōken|Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-momoyama]], south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Meji_Shrine_under_construction_1920.jpg|thumb|Meiji under construction in 1920]] [[File:Emperor-Meiji-Empress-Shoken-Meiji-Shrine-c1926.png|thumb|Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, aerial view of Meiji Jingu, c. 1926.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editor-link1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151|access-date=29 March 2015}} The main timbers came from [[Kiso Mountains|Kiso]] in Nagano, and [[Alishan National Scenic Area#History|Alishan]] in Taiwan, then a Japanese territory, with materials being utilized from every Japanese [[Prefectures of Japan|prefecture]], including [[Karafuto Prefecture|Karafuto]], [[Korea under Japanese rule|Korea]], [[Kwantung Leased Territory|Kwantung]], and [[Taiwan under Japanese rule|Taiwan]]. It was estimated that the cost of the construction was ¥5,219,00 in 1920 (approximately US$26 million [[Tables of historical exchange rates to the United States dollar|today]]), about a quarter of the actual cost due to the donated materials and labor.{{cite journal |last1=Rea |first1=G.B. |title=The Great Meiji Shrine |journal=Far Eastern Review |date=December 1920 |volume=XVI |issue=12 |page=649 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BfG4UYqS9T8C}} It was formally dedicated on November 3, 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926. The interior volume of the shrine complex when originally built was 650 [[Pyeong#Tsubo|tsubo]].{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091029061703/http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archive-date=2009-10-29 |url-status=dead }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first Rank of government-supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[:en:George W. Bush|George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[:en:Hillary Clinton|Hillary Clinton]], and German Foreign Minister [[:en:Guido Westerwelle|Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archive-date=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Naien and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] [[File:Jingu gaien air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Gaien (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The entrances open at sunrise and close at sunset. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[:en:Azekurazukuri|Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the national stadiums ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]], [[National Stadium (Tokyo, 1958)|National Stadium]], and the [[Japan National Stadium (2019)|newer National Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. In February of 2023, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government approved a plan to develop 28.4 hectares of Meiji Jingu Gaien. A new sports stadium, hotel and three skyscrapers are planned for the site. In September 2023, the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS), a UNESCO advisory body, warned of 'irreversible destruction of cultural heritage' if the project, which will result in the loss of 3,000 trees and open park space, is allowed to be completed.{{cite news| url=https://edition.cnn.com/style/tokyo-jingu-gaien-redevelopment-project-hnk-intl/index.html|author=Emiko Jozuka, Francesca Annio, Saki Toi and Daniel Campisi| title=‘Like building skyscrapers in Central Park’: Tokyo redevelopment plan sparks protests| publisher=CNN| date=October 3, 2023}} ==Festivals== Several festivals are held at the shrine per year. Some festivals are held annually. The exhibitions range from ice carving, shodoten (calligraphy winners's works), bonsai, Suiseki Masterpieces, Memory Dolls, Chrysanthemums, Dahlia and exhibitions at the Treasure Museum Annex. * A ring-entering ceremony by a [[Yokozuna]], called {{Nihongo|''Dezuiri''|手数入り}}, is performed at the shrine in January (usually around January 5–7) and during the Autumn Festival. Also newly promoted Yokozuna usually perform their first ring-entering ceremony here.[https://www.meijijingu.or.jp/faq/], Retrieved 2021-02-15.> * Autumn Grand Festival (From October 31 to November 3){{cite web |website=Try Japan |title=Tokyo Sightseeing Area |url=http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |date=October 25, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027175000/http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |archive-date=October 27, 2020}} **October 31 - Autumn Grand Festival Bugaku at {{short description|Shinto shrine in Tokyo, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Meiji Shrine | native_name = 明治神宮 | image = Meiji_Jingu_2023-3.jpg | caption = Meiji Jingu Shrine Main Hall in 2023 | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Imperial Shrine | deity = [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]
[[:en:Empress Shoken|Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''' is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[:en:Empress Shōken|Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-momoyama]], south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Meji_Shrine_under_construction_1920.jpg|thumb|Meiji under construction in 1920]] [[File:Emperor-Meiji-Empress-Shoken-Meiji-Shrine-c1926.png|thumb|Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, aerial view of Meiji Jingu, c. 1926.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[:en:Japanese Diet|Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editor-link1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151|access-date=29 March 2015}} The main timbers came from [[Kiso Mountains|Kiso]] in Nagano, and [[Alishan National Scenic Area#History|Alishan]] in Taiwan, then a Japanese territory, with materials being utilized from every Japanese [[Prefectures of Japan|prefecture]], including [[Karafuto Prefecture|Karafuto]], [[Korea under Japanese rule|Korea]], [[Kwantung Leased Territory|Kwantung]], and [[Taiwan under Japanese rule|Taiwan]]. It was estimated that the cost of the construction was ¥5,219,00 in 1920 (approximately US$26 million [[Tables of historical exchange rates to the United States dollar|today]]), about a quarter of the actual cost due to the donated materials and labor.{{cite journal |last1=Rea |first1=G.B. |title=The Great Meiji Shrine |journal=Far Eastern Review |date=December 1920 |volume=XVI |issue=12 |page=649 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BfG4UYqS9T8C}} It was formally dedicated on November 3, 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926. The interior volume of the shrine complex when originally built was 650 [[Pyeong#Tsubo|tsubo]].{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091029061703/http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archive-date=2009-10-29 |url-status=dead }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first Rank of government-supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[:en:George W. Bush|George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[:en:Hillary Clinton|Hillary Clinton]], and German Foreign Minister [[:en:Guido Westerwelle|Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archive-date=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Naien and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] [[File:Jingu gaien air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Gaien (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The entrances open at sunrise and close at sunset. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[:en:Azekurazukuri|Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the national stadiums ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]], [[National Stadium (Tokyo, 1958)|National Stadium]], and the [[:en:Japan National Stadium (2019)|newer National Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. In February of 2023, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government approved a plan to develop 28.4 hectares of Meiji Jingu Gaien. A new sports stadium, hotel and three skyscrapers are planned for the site. In September 2023, the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS), a UNESCO advisory body, warned of 'irreversible destruction of cultural heritage' if the project, which will result in the loss of 3,000 trees and open park space, is allowed to be completed.{{cite news| url=https://edition.cnn.com/style/tokyo-jingu-gaien-redevelopment-project-hnk-intl/index.html|author=Emiko Jozuka, Francesca Annio, Saki Toi and Daniel Campisi| title=‘Like building skyscrapers in Central Park’: Tokyo redevelopment plan sparks protests| publisher=CNN| date=October 3, 2023}} ==Festivals== Several festivals are held at the shrine per year. Some festivals are held annually. The exhibitions range from ice carving, shodoten (calligraphy winners's works), bonsai, Suiseki Masterpieces, Memory Dolls, Chrysanthemums, Dahlia and exhibitions at the Treasure Museum Annex. * A ring-entering ceremony by a [[Yokozuna]], called {{Nihongo|''Dezuiri''|手数入り}}, is performed at the shrine in January (usually around January 5–7) and during the Autumn Festival. Also newly promoted Yokozuna usually perform their first ring-entering ceremony here.[https://www.meijijingu.or.jp/faq/], Retrieved 2021-02-15.> * Autumn Grand Festival (From October 31 to November 3){{cite web |website=Try Japan |title=Tokyo Sightseeing Area |url=http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |date=October 25, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027175000/http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |archive-date=October 27, 2020}} **October 31 - Autumn Grand Festival Bugaku at the main shrine building **November 1 - Autumn Grand Festival: Enshrinement Anniversary Ceremony, Afternoon Ceremony **November 2 - Autumn Grand Festival Morning Ceremony **November 3 - Autumn Grand {{short description|Shinto shrine in Tokyo, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Meiji Shrine | native_name = 明治神宮 | image = Meiji_Jingu_2023-3.jpg | caption = Meiji Jingu Shrine Main Hall in 2023 | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Imperial Shrine | deity = [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]
[[:en:Empress Shoken|Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''' is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[:en:Empress Shōken|Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-momoyama]], south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Meji_Shrine_under_construction_1920.jpg|thumb|Meiji under construction in 1920]] [[File:Emperor-Meiji-Empress-Shoken-Meiji-Shrine-c1926.png|thumb|Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, aerial view of Meiji Jingu, c. 1926.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[:en:Japanese Diet|Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editor-link1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151|access-date=29 March 2015}} The main timbers came from [[Kiso Mountains|Kiso]] in Nagano, and [[Alishan National Scenic Area#History|Alishan]] in Taiwan, then a Japanese territory, with materials being utilized from every Japanese [[Prefectures of Japan|prefecture]], including [[:en:Karafuto Prefecture|Karafuto]], [[Korea under Japanese rule|Korea]], [[Kwantung Leased Territory|Kwantung]], and [[Taiwan under Japanese rule|Taiwan]]. It was estimated that the cost of the construction was ¥5,219,00 in 1920 (approximately US$26 million [[Tables of historical exchange rates to the United States dollar|today]]), about a quarter of the actual cost due to the donated materials and labor.{{cite journal |last1=Rea |first1=G.B. |title=The Great Meiji Shrine |journal=Far Eastern Review |date=December 1920 |volume=XVI |issue=12 |page=649 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BfG4UYqS9T8C}} It was formally dedicated on November 3, 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926. The interior volume of the shrine complex when originally built was 650 [[Pyeong#Tsubo|tsubo]].{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091029061703/http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archive-date=2009-10-29 |url-status=dead }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first Rank of government-supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[:en:George W. Bush|George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[:en:Hillary Clinton|Hillary Clinton]], and German Foreign Minister [[:en:Guido Westerwelle|Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archive-date=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Naien and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] [[File:Jingu gaien air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Gaien (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[:en:Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The entrances open at sunrise and close at sunset. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[:en:Azekurazukuri|Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the national stadiums ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]], [[National Stadium (Tokyo, 1958)|National Stadium]], and the [[:en:Japan National Stadium (2019)|newer National Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. In February of 2023, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government approved a plan to develop 28.4 hectares of Meiji Jingu Gaien. A new sports stadium, hotel and three skyscrapers are planned for the site. In September 2023, the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS), a UNESCO advisory body, warned of 'irreversible destruction of cultural heritage' if the project, which will result in the loss of 3,000 trees and open park space, is allowed to be completed.{{cite news| url=https://edition.cnn.com/style/tokyo-jingu-gaien-redevelopment-project-hnk-intl/index.html|author=Emiko Jozuka, Francesca Annio, Saki Toi and Daniel Campisi| title=‘Like building skyscrapers in Central Park’: Tokyo redevelopment plan sparks protests| publisher=CNN| date=October 3, 2023}} ==Festivals== Several festivals are held at the shrine per year. Some festivals are held annually. The exhibitions range from ice carving, shodoten (calligraphy winners's works), bonsai, Suiseki Masterpieces, Memory Dolls, Chrysanthemums, Dahlia and exhibitions at the Treasure Museum Annex. * A ring-entering ceremony by a [[Yokozuna]], called {{Nihongo|''Dezuiri''|手数入り}}, is performed at the shrine in January (usually around January 5–7) and during the Autumn Festival. Also newly promoted Yokozuna usually perform their first ring-entering ceremony here.[https://www.meijijingu.or.jp/faq/], Retrieved 2021-02-15.> * Autumn Grand Festival (From October 31 to November 3){{cite web |website=Try Japan |title=Tokyo Sightseeing Area |url=http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |date=October 25, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027175000/http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |archive-date=October 27, 2020}} **October 31 - Autumn Grand Festival Bugaku at the main shrine building **November 1 - Autumn Grand Festival: Enshrinement Anniversary Ceremony, Afternoon Ceremony **November 2 - Autumn Grand Festival Morning Ceremony **November 3 - Autumn Grand {{short description|Shinto shrine in Tokyo, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Meiji Shrine | native_name = 明治神宮 | image = Meiji_Jingu_2023-3.jpg | caption = Meiji Jingu Shrine Main Hall in 2023 | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Imperial Shrine | deity = [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]
[[:en:Empress Shoken|Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''' is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[:en:Empress Shōken|Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-momoyama]], south of [[Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Meji_Shrine_under_construction_1920.jpg|thumb|Meiji under construction in 1920]] [[File:Emperor-Meiji-Empress-Shoken-Meiji-Shrine-c1926.png|thumb|Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, aerial view of Meiji Jingu, c. 1926.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[:en:Japanese Diet|Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editor-link1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151|access-date=29 March 2015}} The main timbers came from [[Kiso Mountains|Kiso]] in Nagano, and [[Alishan National Scenic Area#History|Alishan]] in Taiwan, then a Japanese territory, with materials being utilized from every Japanese [[Prefectures of Japan|prefecture]], including [[:en:Karafuto Prefecture|Karafuto]], [[:en:Korea under Japanese rule|Korea]], [[Kwantung Leased Territory|Kwantung]], and [[Taiwan under Japanese rule|Taiwan]]. It was estimated that the cost of the construction was ¥5,219,00 in 1920 (approximately US$26 million [[Tables of historical exchange rates to the United States dollar|today]]), about a quarter of the actual cost due to the donated materials and labor.{{cite journal |last1=Rea |first1=G.B. |title=The Great Meiji Shrine |journal=Far Eastern Review |date=December 1920 |volume=XVI |issue=12 |page=649 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BfG4UYqS9T8C}} It was formally dedicated on November 3, 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926. The interior volume of the shrine complex when originally built was 650 [[Pyeong#Tsubo|tsubo]].{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091029061703/http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archive-date=2009-10-29 |url-status=dead }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first Rank of government-supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[:en:George W. Bush|George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[:en:Hillary Clinton|Hillary Clinton]], and German Foreign Minister [[:en:Guido Westerwelle|Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archive-date=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Naien and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] [[File:Jingu gaien air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Gaien (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[:en:Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The entrances open at sunrise and close at sunset. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[:en:Azekurazukuri|Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the national stadiums ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]], [[National Stadium (Tokyo, 1958)|National Stadium]], and the [[:en:Japan National Stadium (2019)|newer National Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. In February of 2023, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government approved a plan to develop 28.4 hectares of Meiji Jingu Gaien. A new sports stadium, hotel and three skyscrapers are planned for the site. In September 2023, the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS), a UNESCO advisory body, warned of 'irreversible destruction of cultural heritage' if the project, which will result in the loss of 3,000 trees and open park space, is allowed to be completed.{{cite news| url=https://edition.cnn.com/style/tokyo-jingu-gaien-redevelopment-project-hnk-intl/index.html|author=Emiko Jozuka, Francesca Annio, Saki Toi and Daniel Campisi| title=‘Like building skyscrapers in Central Park’: Tokyo redevelopment plan sparks protests| publisher=CNN| date=October 3, 2023}} ==Festivals== Several festivals are held at the shrine per year. Some festivals are held annually. The exhibitions range from ice carving, shodoten (calligraphy winners's works), bonsai, Suiseki Masterpieces, Memory Dolls, Chrysanthemums, Dahlia and exhibitions at the Treasure Museum Annex. * A ring-entering ceremony by a [[Yokozuna]], called {{Nihongo|''Dezuiri''|手数入り}}, is performed at the shrine in January (usually around January 5–7) and during the Autumn Festival. Also newly promoted Yokozuna usually perform their first ring-entering ceremony here.[https://www.meijijingu.or.jp/faq/], Retrieved 2021-02-15.> * Autumn Grand Festival (From October 31 to November The interior volume of the shrine complex when originally built was 650 [[Pyeong#Tsubo|tsubo]].{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091029061703/http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archive-date=2009-10-29 |url-status=dead }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first Rank of government-supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[:en:George W. Bush|George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[:en:Hillary Clinton|Hillary Clinton]], and German Foreign Minister [[:en:Guido Westerwelle|Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archive-date=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Naien and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] [[File:Jingu gaien air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Gaien (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[:en:Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The entrances open at sunrise and close at sunset. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[:en:Azekurazukuri|Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the national stadiums ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]], [[National Stadium (Tokyo, 1958)|National Stadium]], and the [[:en:Japan National Stadium (2019)|newer National Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. In February of 2023, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government approved a plan to develop 28.4 hectares of Meiji Jingu Gaien. A new sports stadium, hotel and three skyscrapers are planned for the site. In September 2023, the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS), a UNESCO advisory body, warned of 'irreversible destruction of cultural heritage' if the project, which will result in the loss of 3,000 trees and open park space, is allowed to be completed.{{cite news| url=https://edition.cnn.com/style/tokyo-jingu-gaien-redevelopment-project-hnk-intl/index.html|author=Emiko Jozuka, Francesca Annio, Saki Toi and Daniel Campisi| title=‘Like building skyscrapers in Central Park’: Tokyo redevelopment plan sparks protests| publisher=CNN| date=October 3, 2023}} ==Festivals== Several festivals are held at the shrine per year. Some festivals are held annually. The exhibitions range from ice carving, shodoten (calligraphy winners's works), bonsai, Suiseki Masterpieces, Memory Dolls, Chrysanthemums, Dahlia and exhibitions at the Treasure Museum Annex. * A ring-entering ceremony by a [[Yokozuna]], called {{Nihongo|''Dezuiri''|手数入り}}, is performed at the shrine in January (usually around January 5–7) and during the Autumn Festival. Also newly promoted Yokozuna usually perform their first ring-entering ceremony here.[https://www.meijijingu.or.jp/faq/], Retrieved 2021-02-15.> * Autumn Grand Festival (From October 31 to November An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. {{short description|Shinto shrine in Tokyo, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Meiji Shrine | native_name = 明治神宮 | image = Meiji_Jingu_2023-3.jpg | caption = Meiji Jingu Shrine Main Hall in 2023 | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Imperial Shrine | deity = [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]
[[:en:Empress Shoken|Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''' is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[:en:Empress Shōken|Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-momoyama]], south of [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Meji_Shrine_under_construction_1920.jpg|thumb|Meiji under construction in 1920]] [[File:Emperor-Meiji-Empress-Shoken-Meiji-Shrine-c1926.png|thumb|Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, aerial view of Meiji Jingu, c. 1926.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[:en:Japanese Diet|Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editor-link1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151|access-date=29 March 2015}} The main timbers came from [[Kiso Mountains|Kiso]] in Nagano, and [[Alishan National Scenic Area#History|Alishan]] in Taiwan, then a Japanese territory, with materials being utilized from every Japanese [[Prefectures of Japan|prefecture]], including [[:en:Karafuto Prefecture|Karafuto]], [[:en:Korea under Japanese rule|Korea]], [[:en:Kwantung Leased Territory|Kwantung]], and [[Taiwan under Japanese rule|Taiwan]]. It was estimated that the cost of the construction was ¥5,219,00 in 1920 (approximately US$26 million [[Tables of historical exchange rates to the United States dollar|today]]), about a quarter of the actual cost due to the donated materials and labor.{{cite journal |last1=Rea |first1=G.B. |title=The Great Meiji Shrine |journal=Far Eastern Review |date=December 1920 |volume=XVI |issue=12 |page=649 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BfG4UYqS9T8C}} It was formally dedicated on November 3, 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926. The interior volume of the shrine complex when originally built was 650 [[Pyeong#Tsubo|tsubo]].{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091029061703/http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archive-date=2009-10-29 |url-status=dead }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first Rank of government-supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[:en:George W. Bush|George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[:en:Hillary Clinton|Hillary Clinton]], and German Foreign Minister [[:en:Guido Westerwelle|Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archive-date=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Naien and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] [[File:Jingu gaien air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Gaien (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[:en:Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The entrances open at sunrise and close at sunset. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[:en:Azekurazukuri|Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the national stadiums ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]], [[National Stadium (Tokyo, 1958)|National Stadium]], and the [[:en:Japan National Stadium (2019)|newer National Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. In February of 2023, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government approved a plan to develop 28.4 hectares of Meiji Jingu Gaien. A new sports stadium, hotel and three skyscrapers are planned for the site. In September 2023, the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS), a UNESCO advisory body, warned of 'irreversible destruction of cultural heritage' if the project, which will result in the loss of 3,000 trees and open park space, is allowed to be completed.{{cite news| url=https://edition.cnn.com/style/tokyo-jingu-gaien-redevelopment-project-hnk-intl/index.html|author=Emiko Jozuka, Francesca Annio, Saki Toi and Daniel Campisi| title=‘Like building skyscrapers in Central Park’: Tokyo redevelopment plan sparks protests| publisher=CNN| date=October 3, 2023}} ==Festivals== Several festivals are held at the shrine per year. Some festivals are held annually. The exhibitions range from ice carving, shodoten (calligraphy winners's works), bonsai, Suiseki Masterpieces, Memory Dolls, Chrysanthemums, Dahlia and exhibitions at the Treasure Museum Annex. * A ring-entering ceremony by a [[Yokozuna]], called {{Nihongo|''Dezuiri''|手数入り}}, is performed at the shrine in January (usually around January 5–7) and during the Autumn Festival. Also newly promoted Yokozuna usually perform their first ring-entering ceremony here.[https://www.meijijingu.or.jp/faq/], Retrieved 2021-02-15.> * Autumn Grand Festival (From October 31 to November 3){{cite web |website=Try Japan |title=Tokyo Sightseeing Area |url=http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |date=October 25, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027175000/http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |archive-date=October 27, 2020}} **October 31 - Autumn Grand Festival Bugaku at the main shrine building **November 1 - Autumn Grand Festival: Enshrinement Anniversary Ceremony, Afternoon Ceremony **November 2 - Autumn Grand Festival Morning Ceremony **November 3 - Autumn Grand {{short description|Shinto shrine in Tokyo, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Meiji Shrine | native_name = 明治神宮 | image = Meiji_Jingu_2023-3.jpg | caption = Meiji Jingu Shrine Main Hall in 2023 | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Imperial Shrine | deity = [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]
[[:en:Empress Shoken|Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''' is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[:en:Empress Shōken|Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-momoyama]], south of [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Meji_Shrine_under_construction_1920.jpg|thumb|Meiji under construction in 1920]] [[File:Emperor-Meiji-Empress-Shoken-Meiji-Shrine-c1926.png|thumb|Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, aerial view of Meiji Jingu, c. 1926.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[:en:Japanese Diet|Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editor-link1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151|access-date=29 March 2015}} The main timbers came from [[Kiso Mountains|Kiso]] in Nagano, and [[Alishan National Scenic Area#History|Alishan]] in Taiwan, then a Japanese territory, with materials being utilized from every Japanese [[Prefectures of Japan|prefecture]], including [[:en:Karafuto Prefecture|Karafuto]], [[:en:Korea under Japanese rule|Korea]], [[:en:Kwantung Leased Territory|Kwantung]], and [[Taiwan under Japanese rule|Taiwan]]. It was estimated that the cost of the construction was ¥5,219,00 in 1920 (approximately US$26 million [[Tables of historical exchange rates to the United States dollar|today]]), about a quarter of the actual cost due to the donated materials and labor.{{cite journal |last1=Rea |first1=G.B. |title=The Great Meiji Shrine |journal=Far Eastern Review |date=December 1920 |volume=XVI |issue=12 |page=649 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BfG4UYqS9T8C}} It was formally dedicated on November 3, 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926. The interior volume of the shrine complex when originally built was 650 [[Pyeong#Tsubo|tsubo]].{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091029061703/http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archive-date=2009-10-29 |url-status=dead }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first Rank of government-supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[:en:George W. Bush|George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[:en:Hillary Clinton|Hillary Clinton]], and German Foreign Minister [[:en:Guido Westerwelle|Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archive-date=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Naien and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] [[File:Jingu gaien air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Gaien (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[:en:Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The entrances open at sunrise and close at sunset. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[:en:Azekurazukuri|Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the national stadiums ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]], [[National Stadium (Tokyo, 1958)|National Stadium]], and the [[:en:Japan National Stadium (2019)|newer National Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. In February of 2023, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government approved a plan to develop 28.4 hectares of Meiji Jingu Gaien. A new sports stadium, hotel and three skyscrapers are planned for the site. In September 2023, the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS), a UNESCO advisory body, warned of 'irreversible destruction of cultural heritage' if the project, which will result in the loss of 3,000 trees and open park space, is allowed to be completed.{{cite news| url=https://edition.cnn.com/style/tokyo-jingu-gaien-redevelopment-project-hnk-intl/index.html|author=Emiko Jozuka, Francesca Annio, Saki Toi and Daniel Campisi| title=‘Like building skyscrapers in Central Park’: Tokyo redevelopment plan sparks protests| publisher=CNN| date=October 3, 2023}} ==Festivals== Several festivals are held at the shrine per year. Some festivals are held annually. The exhibitions range from ice carving, shodoten (calligraphy winners's works), bonsai, Suiseki Masterpieces, Memory Dolls, Chrysanthemums, Dahlia and exhibitions at the Treasure Museum Annex. * A ring-entering ceremony by a [[Yokozuna]], called {{Nihongo|''Dezuiri''|手数入り}}, is performed at the shrine in January (usually around January 5–7) and during the Autumn Festival. Also newly promoted Yokozuna usually perform their first ring-entering ceremony here.[https://www.meijijingu.or.jp/faq/], Retrieved 2021-02-15.> * Autumn Grand Festival (From October 31 to November 3){{cite web |website=Try Japan |title=Tokyo Sightseeing Area |url=http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |date=October 25, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027175000/http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |archive-date=October 27, 2020}} **October 31 - Autumn Grand Festival Bugaku at the main shrine building **November 1 - Autumn Grand Festival: Enshrinement Anniversary Ceremony, Afternoon Ceremony **November 2 - Autumn Grand Festival Morning Ceremony **November 3 - Autumn Grand Festival Anniversary of Emperor Meiji's Birthday {| class="wikitable" |+ !Festival !Description !Date |- |Oharae |Great purification (to cast out sins and impurities) |December 31, 2020 (Thursday) |- |Joyasai |Year-end ritual |December 31, 2020 (Thursday) |- |Saitaisai |New Year's Day ritual |January 1, 2021 (Friday, National Holiday) |- |Shodoten |Exhibition of winners' works in the calligraphy competition for elementary and junior high school students |from January 5, 2021 (Tuesday) to January 30, 2021 (Saturday) |- |Kigensai |National Foundation Day Festival |February 11, 2021 (Thursday, {{short description|Shinto shrine in Tokyo, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Meiji Shrine | native_name = 明治神宮 | image = Meiji_Jingu_2023-3.jpg | caption = Meiji Jingu Shrine Main Hall in 2023 | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35|40|34|N|139|41|57|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Imperial Shrine | deity = [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]]
[[:en:Empress Shoken|Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''' is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[:en:Empress Shōken|Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-momoyama]], south of [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Meji_Shrine_under_construction_1920.jpg|thumb|Meiji under construction in 1920]] [[File:Emperor-Meiji-Empress-Shoken-Meiji-Shrine-c1926.png|thumb|Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, aerial view of Meiji Jingu, c. 1926.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[:en:Japanese Diet|Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editor-link1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151|access-date=29 March 2015}} The main timbers came from [[Kiso Mountains|Kiso]] in Nagano, and [[Alishan National Scenic Area#History|Alishan]] in Taiwan, then a Japanese territory, with materials being utilized from every Japanese [[Prefectures of Japan|prefecture]], including [[:en:Karafuto Prefecture|Karafuto]], [[:en:Korea under Japanese rule|Korea]], [[:en:Kwantung Leased Territory|Kwantung]], and [[Taiwan under Japanese rule|Taiwan]]. It was estimated that the cost of the construction was ¥5,219,00 in 1920 (approximately US$26 million [[Tables of historical exchange rates to the United States dollar|today]]), about a quarter of the actual cost due to the donated materials and labor.{{cite journal |last1=Rea |first1=G.B. |title=The Great Meiji Shrine |journal=Far Eastern Review |date=December 1920 |volume=XVI |issue=12 |page=649 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BfG4UYqS9T8C}} It was formally dedicated on November 3, 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926. The interior volume of the shrine complex when originally built was 650 [[Pyeong#Tsubo|tsubo]].{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091029061703/http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archive-date=2009-10-29 |url-status=dead }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first Rank of government-supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[:en:George W. Bush|George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[:en:Hillary Clinton|Hillary Clinton]], and German Foreign Minister [[:en:Guido Westerwelle|Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archive-date=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Naien and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] [[File:Jingu gaien air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Gaien (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. This area is covered by an evergreen forest that consists of 120,000 trees of 365 different species, which were donated by people from all parts of Japan when the shrine was established. The forest is visited by many as a recreation and relaxation area in the center of Tokyo. The entrance to the shrine complex leads through the [[:en:Jingu Bashi (Tokyo)|Jingu Bashi]] bridge. Meiji Shrine is adjacent to [[Yoyogi Park]] which together is a large forested area. The entrances open at sunrise and close at sunset. The shrine itself is composed of two major areas: ===Naien=== The Naien is the inner precinct, which is centered on the shrine buildings and includes a treasure museum that houses articles of the Emperor and Empress. The treasure museum is built in the [[:en:Azekurazukuri|Azekurazukuri]] style. ===Gaien=== The Gaien is the outer precinct, which includes the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery that houses a collection of 80 large murals illustrative of the events in the lives of the Emperor and his consort. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the national stadiums ([[Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]], [[National Stadium (Tokyo, 1958)|National Stadium]], and the [[:en:Japan National Stadium (2019)|newer National Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[:en:Meiji Constitution|Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. Today it is used for [[:en:Marriage in Japan|Shinto weddings]] as well as meeting rooms rent and restaurants services. In February of 2023, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government approved a plan to develop 28.4 hectares of Meiji Jingu Gaien. A new sports stadium, hotel and three skyscrapers are planned for the site. In September 2023, the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS), a UNESCO advisory body, warned of 'irreversible destruction of cultural heritage' if the project, which will result in the loss of 3,000 trees and open park space, is allowed to be completed.{{cite news| url=https://edition.cnn.com/style/tokyo-jingu-gaien-redevelopment-project-hnk-intl/index.html|author=Emiko Jozuka, Francesca Annio, Saki Toi and Daniel Campisi| title=‘Like building skyscrapers in Central Park’: Tokyo redevelopment plan sparks protests| publisher=CNN| date=October 3, 2023}} ==Festivals== Several festivals are held at the shrine per year. Some festivals are held annually. The exhibitions range from ice carving, shodoten (calligraphy winners's works), bonsai, Suiseki Masterpieces, Memory Dolls, Chrysanthemums, Dahlia and exhibitions at the Treasure Museum Annex. * A ring-entering ceremony by a [[Yokozuna]], called {{Nihongo|''Dezuiri''|手数入り}}, is performed at the shrine in January (usually around January 5–7) and during the Autumn Festival. Also newly promoted Yokozuna usually perform their first ring-entering ceremony here.[https://www.meijijingu.or.jp/faq/], Retrieved 2021-02-15.> * Autumn Grand Festival (From October 31 to November 3){{cite web |website=Try Japan |title=Tokyo Sightseeing Area |url=http://www.japan-trip.jp/area/shibuya/meiji-jingu-shrine.html |date=October 25, 2020 [[:en:Empress Shoken|Empress Shoken]] | founded_by = | established = November 1, 1920 | date_destroyed = | location = 1-1, Kamizono-chō, [[Yoyogi]], [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]] 151-0053 | website = {{URL|http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} '''{{Nihongo|Meiji Shrine|明治神宮|Meiji Jingū}}''' is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Shibuya]], [[Tokyo]], that is dedicated to the deified spirits of [[:en:Emperor Meiji|Emperor Meiji]] and his wife, [[:en:Empress Shōken|Empress Shōken]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3002.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |title=Introduction |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165144/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11 |publisher=Meiji Jingu}} The shrine does not contain the emperor's grave, which is located at [[Fushimi-ku, Kyoto#Sights|Fushimi-momoyama]], south of [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. ==History== [[File:Meji_Shrine_under_construction_1920.jpg|thumb|Meiji under construction in 1920]] [[File:Emperor-Meiji-Empress-Shoken-Meiji-Shrine-c1926.png|thumb|Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, aerial view of Meiji Jingu, c. 1926.]] After the emperor's death in 1912, the [[:en:Japanese Diet|Japanese Diet]] passed a resolution to commemorate his role in the [[Meiji Restoration]]. An iris garden in an area of Tokyo where Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken had been known to visit was chosen as the building's location. Construction began in 1915 under [[Itō Chūta]], and the shrine was built in the traditional [[nagare-zukuri]] style, using primarily Japanese cypress and copper. The building of the shrine was a national project, mobilizing youth groups and other civic associations from throughout Japan, who contributed labor and funding.{{cite book|editor-link1=James Huffman (historian)|last1=Hardacre|first1=Helen|editor1-last=Huffman|editor1-first=James L.|title=Modern Japan: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Nationalism|chapter=Meiji Shrine|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781135634902|page=151|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWLhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA151|access-date=29 March 2015}} The main timbers came from [[Kiso Mountains|Kiso]] in Nagano, and [[Alishan National Scenic Area#History|Alishan]] in Taiwan, then a Japanese territory, with materials being utilized from every Japanese [[Prefectures of Japan|prefecture]], including [[:en:Karafuto Prefecture|Karafuto]], [[:en:Korea under Japanese rule|Korea]], [[:en:Kwantung Leased Territory|Kwantung]], and [[Taiwan under Japanese rule|Taiwan]]. It was estimated that the cost of the construction was ¥5,219,00 in 1920 (approximately US$26 million [[Tables of historical exchange rates to the United States dollar|today]]), about a quarter of the actual cost due to the donated materials and labor.{{cite journal |last1=Rea |first1=G.B. |title=The Great Meiji Shrine |journal=Far Eastern Review |date=December 1920 |volume=XVI |issue=12 |page=649 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BfG4UYqS9T8C}} It was formally dedicated on November 3, 1920, completed in 1921, and its grounds officially finished by 1926. The interior volume of the shrine complex when originally built was 650 [[Pyeong#Tsubo|tsubo]].{{Cite web|url=http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |title=Meiji Shrine |access-date=2008-03-22 |work=[[Encarta]] |publisher=[[Microsoft]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091029061703/http://encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_761580872/Meiji_Shrine.html |archive-date=2009-10-29 |url-status=dead }} Until 1946, the Meiji Shrine was officially designated one of the ''Kanpei-taisha'' ({{Nihongo2|官幣大社}}), meaning that it stood in the first Rank of government-supported shrines.Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan'', p. 126. The original building was destroyed during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of World War II]]. The present iteration of the shrine was funded through a public fund raising effort and completed in October 1958.{{Cite web|url=http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |title=Shrine Building |access-date=2008-03-22 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080311165139/http://www.meijijingu.or.jp/english/intro/building/index.htm |archive-date = 2008-03-11}} Meiji Shrine has been visited by numerous foreign politicians, including United States President [[:en:George W. Bush|George W. Bush]], United States Secretary of State [[:en:Hillary Clinton|Hillary Clinton]], and German Foreign Minister [[:en:Guido Westerwelle|Guido Westerwelle]].{{cite web|title=Germany and Japan share the same values|url=http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|publisher=Federal Foreign Office, Germany|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207021733/http://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/diplo/en/AAmt/BM-Reisen/2010/01-JapanChina/100114-japan.html|archive-date=2010-02-07|date=14 January 2010}} ==Shrine complex== [[File:Meiji_jingu_yoyogi_park_1989_air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Naien and [[Yoyogi Park]] (1989)]] [[File:Jingu gaien air.jpg|thumb|right|An aerial photograph of Meiji Shrine Gaien (1989)]] Meiji Shrine is located in a forest that covers an area of {{Convert|70|ha|acre}}. It also includes a variety of sports facilities, including the national stadiums ([[:en:Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium|Meiji Jingu Gaien Stadium]], [[National Stadium (Tokyo, 1958)|National Stadium]], and the [[:en:Japan National Stadium (2019)|newer National Stadium]]), and the Meiji Memorial Hall (Meiji Kinenkan), which was originally used for governmental meetings, including discussions surrounding the drafting of the [[:en:Meiji Constitution|Meiji Constitution]] in the late 19th century. In February of 2023, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government approved a plan to develop 28.4 hectares of Meiji Jingu Gaien. A new sports stadium, hotel and three skyscrapers are planned for the site.
